n: In this lecture we will consider the alkaloids that are tropane and quinoline derivatives. According to the outline we will study their toxicological significance and methods of analysis: atropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine and quinine. Key terms: microcrystalloscopic analysis; atropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine, quinine, and gel chromatography. In addition, the lecture covers papaverine, gel chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography, that is, HPLC.

First let us consider the characteristics of the representatives of the group. Atropine is an ester formed by tropine and tropic acid, and is isolated from the belladonna plant. Scopolamine is an ester of scopine and tropic acid; it occurs in henbane. Quinine is a derivative of quinoline and quinuclidine, obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree. Papaverine is an alkaloid identified in opium in 1884. That is, each alkaloid has its own chemical structure and its own source.

Now the structure of atropine. Atropine is an ester formed by tropine and tropic acid, and is obtained from the belladonna plant. Its isomer hyoscyamine differs from atropine in only one feature: it rotates polarised light to the left. Under the action of alkali and high temperature, hyoscyamine quickly loses its optical properties and is converted into atropine. This means that in an alkaline medium and on heating, hyoscyamine passes into atropine.

Solubility of atropine and its use in medicine. As the base, atropine is freely soluble in organic solvents and poorly soluble in water. Atropine sulphate, on the contrary, is freely soluble in water and practically insoluble in organic solvents. In medicine atropine is used in gastric and duodenal ulcer, cholecystitis, gallstones, bronchial asthma, and spasms of the colon and ureters. In ophthalmology it is used to examine the fundus of the eye. Remember: the base and the salt are opposite to each other in solubility.

t: Atropine: indicators in the qualification material
n: Indicators of atropine in the qualification material. Formula C17H23NO3, molecular mass 289.4; it is an anticholinergic drug. Melting point from 114° to 118 °C, pKa 9.9. Solubility is as follows: poorly soluble in water, 1:400; in chloroform 1:1; in diethyl ether 1:60; in ethyl alcohol 1:1. These indicators are used in identifying the substance and distinguishing it from other compounds.

The symptoms of atropine poisoning are characteristic of atropine. First the nervous system is excited: convulsions, accelerated movement, involuntary talking and laughter are observed. Then the endings of the parasympathetic nerves are paralysed: the pupil dilates, the nose becomes dry, and snoring, dryness and flushing of the skin appear. Accidents may occur when children eat large quantities of belladonna berries and nightshade. The pathological-anatomical examination of the corpse is not characteristic.

Absorption, persistence and metabolism of atropine. Atropine is well absorbed through mucous membranes, skin and the intestine. One part is absorbed into the blood, and another binds to serum proteins. Data on its persistence in the body differ: there is the opinion that it is rapidly broken down, and the opinion that it persists for up to 3 weeks or up to 2 years. In the body atropine is broken down to tropic acid and tropine. Of the atropine entering the body, 50 % is excreted unchanged in the urine.

Isolating atropine. Atropine is isolated by extraction with organic solvents in an alkaline medium. From physical evidence it is first extracted with acidified water or alcohol, and then extracted with an organic solvent in an alkaline medium. That is, the sequence is: the object, acidified water or alcohol, alkaline medium, and extraction with an organic solvent.

The Vitali-Morin reaction. If atropine is heated with concentrated HNO3, it breaks down, like an ester, into tropic acid and tropine. As a result, the yellow nitro derivative of tropic acid is formed. If alkali is added to it in the presence of acetone, a violet compound is formed. So the stages of the reaction are: heating, yellow nitro derivative, action of alkali, and violet colour.

The lack of specificity of the Vitali-Morin reaction. This reaction is not characteristic of atropine. It is also given by nitrogenous compounds containing a benzene ring, that is, hyoscyamine, scopolamine, strychnine and apomorphine. Therefore a negative reaction indicates the absence of atropine. A positive reaction, however, requires additional confirmatory reactions. Remember: a negative result is reliable, a positive result is not sufficient.

Confirming atropine: crystal reactions, TLC and UV spectrum. With Reinecke's salt, pink rhomb-shaped crystals are formed. With picric acid, rectangular plates appear. By TLC, Rf=0.26±0.01. In the UV spectrum in alcohol, maxima are observed at 252, 258 and 264 nm. Together, these methods confirm the identity of atropine.

t: Atropine: pharmacological and colour reaction, quantification
n: The pharmacological and colour reactions of atropine and its quantification. In pharmacological testing, atropine dilates the pupil of experimental animals. In the colour reaction with p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde and concentrated H2SO4 it gives a red colour. The amount of atropine is determined by photoelectrocolorimetry, that is, from this red colour, and also from the UV spectrum.

Now scopolamine: source and properties. Scopolamine occurs in henbane; it is an ester of scopine and tropic acid. In medicine scopolamine is used as the bromide. As the base it is a thick, syrupy substance, freely soluble in organic solvents. The salt is freely soluble in water and alcohol, and insoluble in ether and chloroform. It is extracted with organic solvents in an alkaline medium, at pH=8-10. The difference from atropine: by TLC the Rf of scopolamine = 0.44±0.01.

Action and metabolism of scopolamine. Like atropine, it dilates the pupil, relaxes the muscles of the mucous membrane and reduces glandular secretion. “Aeron” tablets are a component of antiemetic and sedative medicines. In the body scopolamine binds well to proteins and is partly hydrolysed. It is broken down mainly in the liver and excreted in the urine.

Identifying scopolamine. Its reactions are similar to those of atropine; now let us look at the distinguishing reactions. With gold hydrobromic acid, liver-coloured, saw-shaped bromaurate is formed. With Reinecke's salt crystals similar to those of atropine are formed, and with Dragendorff's reagent, brown needle-like crystals. By TLC, Rf=0.44±0.01. Scopolamine can be identified by UV and IR spectra, and the amount is found by the extraction-photometric method.

Quinine: source and properties. The alkaloid quinine is a derivative of quinoline and quinuclidine, obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree; it was synthesised in 1944. As the base it is colourless crystals of extremely bitter taste, poorly soluble in water and freely soluble in organic solvents. In medicine, quinine chloride, dihydrochloride and sulphate are used; they are freely soluble in water and bitter. In an alkaline medium, at pH=9-10, quinine passes into the organic solvent layer.

Action and use of quinine. When taken in large amounts, quinine sharply contracts the uterus; women therefore used it for abortion, and accidents occurred. Quinine depresses the central nervous system and the heartbeat, causes headache and dizziness, and weakens vision. In medicine it is used as an antimalarial drug. In obstetrics it is also used to stimulate and strengthen labour.

Metabolism and fluorescence of quinine. In the body the quinoline and quinuclidine nuclei are oxidised: 2-oxyquinine, dioxyquinine and others are formed. The metabolites and unbound quinine are excreted in the urine. If UV light is directed at a solution in sulphuric acid, a bright blue fluorescence is seen; the chloride ion reduces it. When ammonia is added, at pH=9, the blue colour disappears and violet fluorescence appears.

The thalleioquin reaction of quinine. The quinine residue, under the action of bromine water and ammonia, forms green thalleioquin, which passes into chloroform. The sequence: quinine and bromine water, then ammonia, then extraction with chloroform. Excess bromine, antipyrine and amidopyrine interfere with the reaction. In 1967 thalleioquin was studied by elemental analysis and IR and UV spectra, and a chemical formula was proposed.

t: Quinine: erythroquin reaction, TLC and UV
n: Quinine: the erythroquin reaction, TLC and UV spectrum. In the erythroquin reaction, bromine water and yellow prussiate of potash are added, then an alkaline medium is created with ammonia; as a result a pink colour appears. In TLC a mixture of ether, acetone and ammonia in the ratio 40:20:2 is used; the confirmatory reagent is Dragendorff's, Rf=0.39. In the UV spectrum in alcohol the maxima are at 236, 278 and 332 nm.

Extraction-photometric determination of quinine. The alkaloid forms a complex, tropaeolinate, with the acidic dye tropaeolin 00 at pH=4.6. This complex passes into chloroform. Then, on hydrolysis in methyl alcohol and H2SO4, it gives raspberry-coloured tropaeolin. The intensity of the colour depends on the amount of quinine, so the amount is determined by photoelectrocolorimetry.

Now the principle of gel chromatography. In gel chromatography the same solvent is used as the mobile and as the stationary phase. The part of the solvent moving along the flow is the mobile phase. The part absorbed into the pores of the gel serves as the stationary phase. Gels were first used for liquid mixtures in 1959 by Porath and Flodin.

The order of separation in gel chromatography. Molecules of small size are absorbed into the pores of the gel and retained. Large molecules move with the solvent between the particles. Therefore the molecules of large size are washed out first, and the small ones after them. The method is simple, fast and separates under much milder conditions than other types of chromatography. Additional adsorption and chemical factors also have an effect; they are taken into account when choosing conditions.

t: Gel chromatography: two kinds of interaction
n: Two kinds of interaction in gel chromatography. If the components have the same molecular mass, separation is based on the difference in interaction between the substance and the gel phase. The first: the force of interaction between the charged molecule being separated and charged particles. The second: the action of ionogenic groups associated with substances dissolved in the swollen gel phase, as a dispersive force of the gel shell. Gel chromatography is used in column and thin-layer forms.

Types of gels. Soft gels absorb the solvent and swell; they include Sephadex, polyacrylamide and starch. Semi-rigid gels increase in volume 1.1-1.8 times on swelling; styrogels are an example. Rigid gels, that is, silica gel and porous glass, do not change their volume. Thus the types differ in solvent uptake and change in volume.

Advantages and disadvantages of rigid gels. Rigid gels include silica gel and porous glass. Their pores are constant, and the volume does not change under any conditions. They show high permeability. The first disadvantage: silicates contain hydroxyl groups. The second disadvantage: their leachability is greater than that of soft and semi-rigid gels.

Soft and semi-rigid gels. Soft gels are high-molecular organic compounds with few lateral bonds; they swell, absorbing a lot of solvent. They are used for separating low-molecular substances at a low flow rate, more often in thin-layer chromatography. Chromatography on soft gels is usually called gel filtration; it has high efficiency. Semi-rigid gels are obtained by polymerisation, are resistant to pressure, do not deform and are hydrophobic.

The solvent and column in gel chromatography. The solvent must dissolve the mixture and wet the gel surface, but not be absorbed into it. For a soft gel it must swell the gel and must not be viscous. The soft gel is first swollen in the separating solvent; the semi-rigid gel is packed as a suspension, that is, a slurry. The inner diameter of the column is 8-10 mm; increasing it to 50 mm raises efficiency, while reducing it is not recommended.

Papaverine: source and physical properties. Papaverine was identified in opium in 1884; opium contains about 0.1-1.5 %, and it has also been obtained synthetically. As the base it forms colourless crystals in the shape of rhombi or needles, melting point 147 °C; insoluble in water, soluble in hot alcohol and chloroform. It has weakly basic properties, and therefore sometimes passes into the chloroform layer even under acidic conditions. Papaverine hydrochloride is a white powder, freely soluble in water, 1:40; melting point 225-226 °C.

Toxicological significance and metabolism of papaverine. Papaverine dilates blood vessels and has an antispasmodic effect; in larger amounts it has a sedative effect, and has no narcotic effect. Its toxic effect is weaker than that of morphine, the maximum dose is 0.1 g. Metabolism consists mainly of demethylation of the methyl radicals: phenolic compounds are excreted in the urine as glucuronides. In isolation it must be sought in both the acidic and alkaline chloroform solutions.

Isolation and quantification of papaverine. In forensic chemistry, papaverine must be sought in both the acidic and the alkaline chloroform solutions. The reason is that, owing to its weakly basic character, it sometimes passes into the chloroform layer even under acidic conditions. The amount of papaverine is determined spectrophotometrically from the UV spectrum. IR spectrum peaks: 1507, 1068 and 1273 cm⁻¹.

Identification reactions of papaverine. With Marquis, Fröhde and Erdmann reagents a characteristic red colour is formed. If a drop of 10 % cadmium chloride is added to a residue dissolved in 0.1 N HCl, colourless crystals in the form of cubic plates appear. With iodine solution it also gives a red colour; sensitivity 0.1 µg. In the UV spectrum in 0.1 N HCl the maxima are at 250, 284 and 310 nm.

The Sobolev reaction for papaverine and spectra. Under the action of Marquis reagent, methylenebis-papaverine is formed. It is oxidised by bromine water, and on addition of ammonia gives a stable violet colour. The reaction is very sensitive and is recommended also for determining the amount of papaverine in physical evidence. In TLC, in the codeine system, Rf=0.75; UV spectrum in 0.1 N HCl 250, 284, 310 nm; IR spectrum 1507, 1068, 1273 cm⁻¹.

Papaverine and narcotine: weak bases. The isolate obtained under acidic conditions is examined for alkaloids with weakly basic properties: caffeine, theobromine, theophylline, papaverine, narcotine and strychnine. In purification by re-extraction, substances with weakly basic properties are lost; these are purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine. The book has no separate section on narcotine, and no reaction or spectral data are given.

Now the principle of HPLC, that is, high-performance liquid chromatography. The mobile phase, the eluent, passes through the sorbent in the column at high speed under high pressure. The method makes it possible to separate high- and low-molecular, thermolabile substances and to determine their identity and amount. The parts of the chromatograph: a high-performance column, an injector, a high-pressure pump, a detector with a recording device, and a microprocessor.

The design of the HPLC instrument. The pump delivers the eluent at a constant rate: up to 200-500 atm; in microcolumn chromatographs up to 1-20 atm. The column is of steel or glass: length 10-25 cm, inner diameter 0.3-0.8 cm; particle size 5-10 µm. The column temperature is maintained to within ±0.1 °C; separation is most often carried out at 20-25 °C. The sequence of parts: eluent reservoir, pump, sample injection, column and detector.

Detectors and adsorbents in HPLC. Detectors: refractometric or fluorimetric, spectrophotometric, 190-900 nm or most often 254 nm, and mass-spectrometric. As the adsorbent, silica gel with hydroxyl groups, silica gel treated with functional groups, aluminium oxide and polymers are used. On silica gel the eluent is hydrocarbons, while on silica gel with hydrophobic groups it is aqueous solutions containing lower alcohols or acetonitrile.

t: HPLC: types of separation and evaluating the result
n: Types of separation in HPLC and evaluating the result. Ion-pair chromatography separates organic compounds in the form of salts, acids and bases, while ion-exchange chromatography separates anions and cations. In the same medium, the time at which a substance leaves the column is the same and constant; this is used to establish identity. In quantitative analysis the peak areas are calculated, because the peak area is directly proportional to the amount of substance.

Now let us compare the TLC and UV indicators. Atropine: Rf=0.26±0.01; UV maxima 252, 258, 264 nm in alcohol. Scopolamine: Rf=0.44±0.01, no UV indicator in the book. Quinine: Rf=0.39, in the system ether, acetone and ammonia 40:20:2; UV maxima in alcohol 236, 278, 332 nm. Papaverine: UV maxima in 0.1 N HCl 250, 284, 310 nm, Rf=0.75.

The general scheme of analysis. First stage: isolation with an organic solvent in an alkaline medium; pH=8-10 for scopolamine, pH=9-10 for quinine. Then confirmation: precipitating reagents, Vitali-Morin, crystal reactions, thalleioquin and erythroquin. Then TLC, UV and IR spectra, and HPLC are used. The amount is determined by photoelectrocolorimetry, the UV spectrum and extraction photometry.

Conclusion. Atropine and hyoscyamine are esters of tropine and tropic acid. The Vitali-Morin reaction is non-specific, but a negative result means the absence of atropine. For quinine, blue fluorescence, the thalleioquin reaction, green, and the erythroquin reaction, pink, are characteristic; the amount is determined by extraction photometry with tropaeolin 00. Gel chromatography separates by molecular size, and HPLC separates under high pressure with a detector; papaverine is identified by the Sobolev reaction.
